newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela stock gains seen in '97 despite stumble.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela stock gains seen in '97 despite stumble.

text.p: Venezuela's flagging stock market may be the region's worst performer so far this year, but analysts still expect the bolsa to post solid gains by the end of 1997 after a spectacular rise last year.

"We believe the market has not entirely factored in recent significant advances," said Jose Corral, regional chief analyst for Santander Investments, who sees a 32 percent rise in dollar terms for the index by the end of the year, despite a nearly eight percent drop so far in 1997.

Those advances include a slowing of inflation in March to 1.6 percent -- the lowest in five years -- and a recent ground-breaking agreement to reform the country's crumbling social security and severance pay system.
That agreement, currently under discussion in Congress, is expected to free up Venezuela's rigid labor markets, reduce company labor costs and boost productivity throughout the economy, analysts say.
When the agreement was announced on March 17, it left the market impressively unmoved.

"Although frustrating to market analysts and participants, the (lack of) reaction is comprehensible. There aren't that many attractive stocks to buy on the stock market -- today," wrote InvestAnalysis consultant Alex Dalmady in a recent market commentary.
Last year's 100 percent run-up in equity prices left Venezuelan stocks fully valued, analysts say, with little upside potential.
Still, over the long run, many businesses stand to benefit from the social security reform -- which also envisages Chilean-style private pension funds -- and stock prices may not yet reflect that.

"The payout required to liquidate the old (social security) system should drive up credit demand. ...Real estate prices could benefit as employees look for ways to invest the lump sums.... Consumer products and services should also benefit from higher take-home pay," wrote Dalmady.
Social security reform is also not the kind of snappy, unequivocal signal that many foreign investors look for before committing funds, analysts say.

It's better to have something clear-cut and punchy, such as the slated $3 billion privatization of state holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana's (CVG) aluminum and steel companies, scheduled for later this year.
"The dedicated funds are already in Venezuelan equities and Brady bonds, said Santander's Corral.
"What the market needs to move again are the non-dedicated funds, and what they need to swing in are clearer-cut reform signals, such as CVG's privatization," he said.
Over the short term, however, the Caracas bolsa looks to remain bumpy, while investors remain focused on unsettled U.S. stock and bond markets.

"The IBC index has been taking a hit in recent days. ... While we maintain the economic fundamentals do not suggest this trend will continue in the medium term, a strong break of 6080 key support would be ... more worrisome," said New York-based IDEA in a recent market comment.
"On a technical basis, the recent break of 6250 support places the IBC in clear sight of critical 6080," IDEA added.
On Tuesday, the bolsa closed slightly ahead at 6,201.31 points, according to preliminary figures from the exchange.
